title: Market Risk, Lesson 2: VaR backtesting - counting how often the model is wrong
subtitle: Expected breaches, the Kupiec test, the Basel traffic-light system and the clustering trap
whyItMatters: A VaR model that has never been backtested is a claim with no evidence behind it. It is also the point where the regulator intervenes directly: the number of breaches sets the bank's capital multiplier, so it has consequences in real money.
openingQuestion: A one-day 99% VaR. Across 250 trading days, how many losses exceeding VaR are normal?
openingOptions: None at all - breaching VaR means the model is wrong
About 2 to 3 times, since 1% of 250 days is 2.5
It cannot be determined without knowing the portfolio size
explanation: This is the most common misunderstanding about VaR. A 99% level means the model expects to be breached on 1% of days - roughly 2 to 3 times in 250 trading days. No breaches at all is not a good sign but a sign the model is too conservative, and that a bank is holding too much capital against risk that is not there. Too many breaches means the model is understating risk. Backtesting is the exercise of comparing the actual breach count against the expected count and asking whether the gap is larger than chance allows.

diagram.label: Count the days where the loss exceeds VaR
Compare against the expected count: 1% × number of days
Kupiec test: is the gap significant?

realWorldExample.company: The traffic-light system and the capital multiplier
realWorldExample.description: The Basel framework sorts backtesting results into three zones by breach count over 250 days: the green zone is acceptable, the yellow zone requires explanation, the red zone forces a model rebuild. The important part is that the consequence does not stop at a reminder - the more breaches, the higher the multiplier applied to the capital requirement, meaning the bank has to hold more capital against the same portfolio. This is one of the few places where the quality of a statistical model converts directly into a cost of capital.

quiz.question: What does having no VaR breaches at all in a year tell you?
options: The model may be too conservative, holding capital against risk that is not really there
The model is working perfectly and needs no adjustment in the next review
The portfolio is fully hedged and no longer carries any market risk at all
The input data must have been corrupted during collection and processing
quiz.explanation: Capital is a resource with a cost. A model that is too conservative is not safer, it is only more expensive - and in a backtest it counts as a deviation that needs fixing just as much as the opposite one. A zero count is not evidence of perfection, no real portfolio is free of market risk, and clean data can perfectly well produce zero breaches if the VaR numbers were simply set too high.

quiz.question: What question does the Kupiec test answer?
options: Whether breaches tend to appear close together in the same stretch of time
Whether the observed breach count strays further than chance allows
What the average loss on days beyond the VaR threshold is against that threshold
Which of three VaR methods comes closest to reality on the same portfolio
quiz.explanation: This is a test of frequency, and it looks only at the total number of breaches. It has no interest whatsoever in when those breaches occurred, which is why an independence test is run alongside it rather than instead of it. It says nothing about how deep the losses ran past the threshold - that is what expected shortfall is for - and it does not rank one VaR method against another.

quiz.question: Why are clustered breaches more worrying than evenly spread ones?
options: Because the Basel framework counts only consecutive breaches for the multiplier
Because consecutive breaches always carry a larger loss than isolated ones
Because it shows the model misses a change in volatility regime, not just random error
Because spread breaches are normal while clustered breaches signal fraud
quiz.explanation: The right number of breaches all falling in two crisis weeks means the model is only right while markets are calm - which is to say, wrong exactly when it is needed most. Basel counts every breach in the window regardless of adjacency, the size of the loss is a separate question from its timing, and clustering points to a modelling weakness rather than to any misconduct.

quiz.question: Why does backtesting use a hypothetical loss rather than that day's actual loss?
options: Because the regulator does not permit actual profit and loss data in internal model validation
Because the actual loss is only fixed once the accounting period closes
Because the hypothetical loss is always larger and so gives a more prudent result
Because the actual loss includes intraday trading and fees, not the risk of the opening book
quiz.explanation: VaR measures the risk of the book as it stood at the start of the day, held unchanged. Mixing the intraday trading result into it tests two different things at once. Actual profit and loss is available daily and regulators do use it in a complementary test, and there is no rule that the hypothetical figure is the larger of the two - it can easily be smaller on a day when the desk traded well.

quiz.question: Why does backtesting use a hypothetical loss on an unchanged book instead of the actual loss made during the day?
options: Because the actual loss also contains intraday trading, not the risk the model measures
Because the actual loss is only determined once the financial reporting period has closed
Because the regulator does not allow a bank's actual loss figures to be used
Because the hypothetical loss is always larger and gives a more prudent result
quiz.explanation: VaR forecasts for the book as it stood at the opening. If the trader has been buying and selling all session, the end-of-day loss reflects those decisions as well as the market move - and mixing the two means you are no longer testing the model itself. The reporting period has nothing to do with it, since the figure is produced daily, and no rule bars actual loss data from being used in a separate complementary test.

keyTakeaways: A 99% VaR expects to be breached roughly 2-3 times in 250 days - never being breached is a problem too
Kupiec tests frequency: does the breach count stray further than chance allows
Clustered breaches are more dangerous than evenly spread ones, even at the same total
Basel converts the test result into a capital multiplier - the consequence is measured in money
Use the hypothetical loss on the opening book, not the actual loss that includes intraday trading

practicePrompt.question: A 99% VaR model shows 3 breaches in 250 days, but all 3 fall in the same week. What do you conclude?
options: The model passes, since 3 breaches sit inside the expected range
Frequency passes but distribution fails: the breaches cluster
The model is too conservative
The data window needs extending to 500 days
practicePrompt.explanation: This is exactly why a Kupiec-style frequency test is a necessary condition and not a sufficient one. Three breaches in 250 days is entirely normal in count, but packing them into one week means the model does not react when the volatility regime shifts - it produced a low number all through the calm stretch and went on producing a low number once the market had already moved. The next lesson on EWMA and GARCH exists precisely to deal with this.

summary.keyIdea: A risk model has to prove it is right, and the evidence is the count of how often it was wrong
summary.commonMistake: Treating the absence of any breach as a sign of a good model
summary.action: Take a VaR series and the realised returns, count the breaches, and plot them over time to see whether they cluster.

application.title: What to do
application.message: Take two years of return data, compute a 99% VaR rolling over a 250-day window, then mark every day where the loss exceeded VaR. Count the total and plot their positions along the time axis. Compare that count against the expected 1%.
application.secondary: If the marks bunch around a few periods, you have just reconstructed by hand the reason Basel does not stop at counting frequency.

sections.text: Every model makes a claim about the future. Backtesting is the only mechanism that forces that claim to face what actually happened.

left.label: Is the frequency right
left.text: Is the breach count close to the expected level? The Kupiec test answers this one. Too many and the model understates risk; too few and it is making the desk hold surplus capital.

right.label: Is the distribution right
right.text: Are the breaches independent of one another, or do they cluster? Clustering signals a model that does not update fast enough when the volatility regime changes - exactly when it needs to be right.

sections.label: Why the hypothetical loss
sections.text: Backtesting does not compare VaR against that day's actual profit and loss, but against a hypothetical loss: hold the opening book unchanged and revalue it at the day's market moves. The reason is that actual profit and loss also contains intraday buying and selling, fees and commissions - none of which VaR measures. Mixing them in lets a desk with a good trading day mask a bad risk model.
The Basel traffic light: from breach count to capital

For a 99% confidence VaR over a 250 trading day window, the expected breach count is 250 × 1% = 2.5 a year. Nobody expects exactly 2.5 - the question is how far is far enough to conclude the model is wrong rather than unlucky. Basel answers with three zones: 0 to 4 breaches is green, 5 to 9 is yellow, 10 or more is red. What gives the mechanism teeth is the capital multiplier attached: green keeps the multiplier at 3.0; yellow rises gradually from 3.4 at 5 breaches to 3.85 at 9; red is 4.0. A poorly calibrated model is not merely noted - it directly raises the capital that has to be held.

sections.label: Why 4 and 5 breaches differ so much
sections.text: Not because one extra breach carries great economic meaning, but because the line has to be drawn somewhere and the yellow zone is designed to shift incentives. In the yellow zone the burden of proof reverses: the bank has to explain why the model is still trustworthy, instead of the regulator having to prove it is broken. With 250 observations, a correct model still has a meaningful chance of landing in yellow - that is the price of a small sample, and the reason the yellow zone is not automatically a breach of the rules.

Counting breaches answers only half the question. The other half is whether they are spread out or bunched. Four breaches spread across the year sit comfortably in green; four breaches falling on four consecutive days also sit in green, but they say the model does not update fast enough when volatility steps up - exactly the kind of failure that does the most damage. That is why an independence test on the breaches runs in parallel with the frequency test, rather than replacing it.

lines: A model that has never been wrong is not necessarily good - it is more likely just expensive.
The next lesson covers the weakness backtesting cannot detect: VaR does not tell you how large the loss is once it is breached.
